dailyBrief.text: Good morning — the warm spell is over: Solon turns partly cloudy and much cooler today, high near 56° after yesterday's 76°, with a chilly low around 38° tonight. Overnight, Iran said four oil tankers hit mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after the U.S. said the main lanes were cleared, and Binance disclosed a $6.3 billion hack, the biggest theft in crypto history. The Cavs rallied late but fell 114-111 at Atlanta — Harden had 24 and Mitchell 22 — and they're back at it Halloween night in Milwaukee. Today locally, early in-person voting runs 7:30 AM to 7:30 PM, Jurassic Quest opens downtown, and Pumpkins & Piranhas has its final night at the aquarium.

Iran says four oil tankers hit mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary:
Iran's armed forces said on Thursday that four oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines in or near the Strait of Hormuz. The Revolutionary Guards said three of the ships had exploded in the previous 24 hours while using what Tehran calls an unauthorised southern route through the strait, adding that the vessels had switched off their radar and navigation systems and ignored warnings. Iran's army later reported a fourth tanker on fire east of the strait.

The claim landed one day after the U.S. military said it had cleared the main shipping lanes of mines. A Revolutionary Guards spokesman publicly challenged Washington to prove that with independent evidence rather than statements. Britain's UK Maritime Trade Operations agency, meanwhile, reported its own incidents in the same waters, including a vessel on fire northeast of Khasab, Oman, a tanker hit by an unknown projectile, and a traditional dhow that caught fire and sank.

The strait is the world's most important oil chokepoint, carrying roughly a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas, so competing claims about whether it is safe go straight to energy prices. U.S. Central Command insists the primary transit routes have been swept; Iran insists the southern corridor is mined and that crews use it at their own risk.

Watch for independent confirmation of the tanker incidents and for oil prices, which rose on Friday as traders weighed the risk to shipments.

items.title: Spain mourns 69 dead in its second deadly train crash of the year
items.summary:
Spain has begun three days of national mourning after a high-speed Renfe train slammed into the back of a stationary Iryo train near Urda, in Toledo province, on Wednesday morning. One more body was found overnight, lifting the death toll to 69, with about 50 people still in hospital. The two trains were carrying 544 passengers between them on the Madrid to Seville line.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash followed a computer malfunction that knocked out the safety system along a 63-kilometre stretch at about 8:30 a.m., automatically stopping every train. A central command centre then told the Renfe train to start moving again, without speed restrictions and despite an active stop signal, and it hit the stopped train at 8:53 a.m., possibly travelling as fast as 200 km/h. Puente said the drivers were not to blame and called the order inexplicable; the controller involved has been questioned.

It is Spain's second deadly high-speed crash in nine months, after 46 people died at Adamuz in January on trains run by the same two companies, and the deadliest rail disaster since 2013. King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited survivors in a Toledo hospital, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who faces a general election on November 29, called two disasters in one year unacceptable for a rail network that was once a source of national pride.

Separate judicial and government investigations are now running, alongside a previously planned drivers' strike over rail-safety investment.

items.title: Italian peacekeeping helicopter crashes in Bosnia, killing four
items.summary:
An Italian Army CH-47 Chinook helicopter working with the European Union's peacekeeping mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina crashed during a routine training flight on Thursday, killing four people and injuring 11. Italy's defence ministry said two of the dead were Italian Army soldiers and two belonged to the Italian Red Cross's Volunteer Military Corps. All 15 people aboard were accounted for, and the injured were described as stable.

The helicopter came down in the village of Gorice, in the Brčko district in the country's northeast, about 180 kilometres from Sarajevo. EUFOR, the EU force, said no civilians were hurt and no property was damaged on the ground. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed condolences to the families.

The aircraft was deployed under Operation Althea, the EU mission that oversees implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement, which ended the Bosnian war in 1995 and still underpins the country's fragile politics. Italy is one of the mission's main contributors.

Investigators have begun work to establish what brought the helicopter down. Neither the Italian ministry nor EUFOR has pointed to any cause — mechanical, weather or human — so far.

items.title: Ukraine pauses its strikes on Russian oil refineries after pressure from Trump
items.summary:
Ukraine's military has paused its long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries after weeks of pressure from President Trump, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday. Ukrainian strike units were told in mid-October to wind down the campaign once missions already in motion were finished, and the unofficial pause is expected to last at least until after Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, and possibly deeper into November.

Kyiv had resisted the demand for months, arguing that hitting refineries — which fund Russia's war and supply its army — is its most effective answer to years of Russian bombardment. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that his forces have no formal order to avoid refineries, and noted Ukraine had already observed one 72-hour pause earlier in October while Russia kept striking Ukraine's energy grid. The pressure campaign, as reported, also included restrictions on Ukraine's military Starlink service and warnings about U.S. intelligence sharing.

The refinery campaign had real bite: fuel shortages forced sales restrictions across swathes of Russia over the summer, and Russian outlets reported this week that free fuel sales have resumed in 15 regions as the strikes slowed.

Reuters said it could not immediately verify the Journal's account. Watch whether the pause holds after the midterms, and whether Russia eases its own strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure in return.

items.title: North Korea fires about 10 missiles as a landmine dispute with the South worsens
items.summary:
North Korea fired roughly 10 short-range ballistic missiles from around Wonsan on its east coast into the sea toward Japan at about 12:30 p.m. on Thursday, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said. The missiles flew about 250 kilometres. Japan confirmed at least one projectile fell outside its exclusive economic zone, and no damage was reported.

It was Pyongyang's 17th ballistic missile event of 2026 and its first in 17 days. Seoul's presidential National Security Office held an emergency meeting, condemned the launches as violations of UN Security Council resolutions, and stepped up surveillance alongside the United States and Japan.

The volley comes on top of a deteriorating border dispute. A September 21 landmine explosion in the Demilitarized Zone injured three South Korean soldiers — one lost an ankle — and a joint South Korean and UN investigation concluded the mines were planted by the North more than a year ago, slightly south of the military demarcation line. Seoul demanded an apology.

Pyongyang denies planting the mines and this week accused Seoul of fabricating the blast in a letter to the Security Council. It has also not answered South Korea's October 23 proposal for military talks, and South Korean experts say Northern artillery has been seen moving closer to the border — a mix that raises the risk of a clash neither side says it wants.

items.title: Last Ebola patients leave a Congo treatment centre, but the outbreak is far from over
items.summary:
Healthcare workers in Mongbwalu, in Congo's Ituri province, sang and danced this week as the last patients were discharged from the Ebola treatment centre there. The facility, run by Doctors Without Borders, has no confirmed cases under treatment for the first time since the outbreak was declared on May 15 — a genuine milestone in the place where the outbreak began.

The wider picture is still grim. Government data released Tuesday put confirmed cases above 10,000, making this the fastest-growing and deadliest Ebola outbreak in Congo's history, with nearly half of those infected having died. At least 2,600 patients have recovered. The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment, and it has spread to 66 health zones across eight provinces.

Response teams are working against serious headwinds: most new cases are appearing outside the list of monitored contacts, some local responders recently struck over bonuses unpaid since August, and health workers have been attacked — a nurse was killed last week while answering an Ebola alert.

African health ministers held a virtual summit this week to coordinate the response. As the WHO's director-general put it, the outbreak is far from over, but every life saved is worth celebrating.

items.title: Pentagon's fired top planner admitted leaking Iran and Ukraine secrets, report says
items.summary:
Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, until this week the Pentagon's top military planner, admitted to leaking classified information about the wars in Ukraine and Iran to journalists from two separate outlets over the course of about a year, according to an internal investigation report obtained by Axios. Sylvia acknowledged the disclosures in a recorded interview after failing four polygraph tests, a U.S. official told Axios.

Sylvia held the Joint Staff's J5 job — director of strategy, plans and policy — placing him at the centre of U.S. military planning for both conflicts. The investigation found the disclosures began as early as June 2025 and continued through messages on the encrypted Signal app and an in-person meeting at a diner in Arlington, Virginia, held after one journalist's Pentagon access had been withdrawn. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from the post this week.

A Pentagon spokesman said the department has zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorised disclosure of classified information. The case has now been referred to the Justice Department, which will decide whether to bring charges; Sylvia has not publicly responded, and the admissions come from an investigative record, not a court plea.

It is the most senior leak case yet in the administration's crackdown on unauthorised disclosures and restricted press access at the Pentagon.

items.title: Alaska's governor won't promise to certify the Senate result if the Democrat wins
items.summary:
Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy declined on Thursday to say he would certify the state's U.S. Senate result if Democrat Mary Peltola wins, telling NewsNation the state would follow the law but would not send what he called a "scam" to Washington. He said findings of illegality could affect whether the winner is seated.

The fight centres on a second candidate named Dan Sullivan. Reporting by The New York Times this week alleged that Peltola campaign staff and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee aides helped recruit spoiler candidates — including Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg — to siphon votes from incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. Peltola says she knew nothing about any such effort, and the second Sullivan denies involvement with her campaign. Alaska's Supreme Court ruled this spring that he stays on the ballot.

Dunleavy has ordered the state Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the alleged recruitment broke state law, and the Justice Department has issued subpoenas and sued to block certification of a Peltola victory while the second Sullivan remains a candidate. The state itself is fighting that federal suit.

With the Senate's balance of power in play, a certification standoff could run past Dunleavy's own term, which ends December 7 — days after Alaska's target certification date.

items.title: Judge blocks the Justice Department from setting aside 20,000 California ballots
items.summary:
A federal judge in Los Angeles on Wednesday refused the Trump Justice Department's emergency request to force California to segregate mail ballots tied to about 20,000 people the government calls "likely" noncitizens. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter wrote that granting the order would "wreak havoc" on an election already underway, create a chilling effect on voters and election workers, and discount the votes of U.S. citizens.

The Justice Department sued California in mid-October, saying officials missed a 48-hour deadline to review its list — delivered on a password-protected thumb drive — and that counting ineligible votes dilutes citizens' ballots. Carter found the list not credible, pointing to duplicates, cancelled registrations and records showing U.S. birthplaces, and noted that more than 3.7 million Californians had already voted. Federal law does bar noncitizens from voting; Carter said the lawful remedy is prosecution, and the department has already charged 28 people this month.

The ruling is the latest courtroom setback for the administration's push for federal oversight of state-run elections days before the midterms. A federal appeals panel had already rejected an earlier version of the same request, 2-1.

The Justice Department immediately appealed to the Ninth Circuit and said it would seek emergency relief, and it filed a similar request this week in Washington state.

items.title: Trump cancels weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa and switches to phone rallies
items.summary:
President Trump has cancelled his planned weekend rallies in Salina, Kansas, and Dubuque, Iowa — two states with unexpectedly competitive Senate races — less than a week before the midterm elections. The Republican National Committee announced the change on Thursday, saying tele-rallies would let the president reach more voters in the limited time left; a Trump-aligned group says he will phone into events in at least 19 states.

The president will still hold one more in-person rally, in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday. Since October 1 he has held 25 rallies in 19 states. Asked about Kansas, Trump told reporters he did not feel he had to go, expressing confidence in Republican Senator Roger Marshall — and erupted at the question in the process.

The cancellations come as polling in Kansas has tightened: a CNN/SSRS survey of likely voters conducted October 20–26 put Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton four points ahead of Marshall, 49% to 45%. Marshall told reporters he did not know exactly why the rally was cancelled. Both he and Iowa's candidates have at times kept some distance from the president during the campaign.

Tuesday's results will decide whether Republicans keep their narrow control of the Senate and House for the rest of Trump's term.

items.title: U.S. weighs new Iran strikes while mediators push Tehran toward a nuclear deal
items.summary:
President Trump held an extraordinary meeting with senior military officials at the White House as the administration weighs a possible new campaign against Iran, the Wall Street Journal reported. At the same time, a diplomatic track is moving: Vice President JD Vance has sent a letter to Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary seeking to revive peace talks.

According to Axios, Qatar-led mediators are pressing Iran to accept nuclear concessions to head off massive U.S.-Israeli strikes after the midterms. The proposal would give UN inspectors access to Iran's bombed nuclear facilities in exchange for limited sanctions relief and access to frozen funds, and Iran's side is expected to seek Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's approval in the coming days. Separately, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged ordinary Iranians to withhold taxes and stock up on fuel for the winter.

The military commander for the Middle East, Adm. Brad Cooper, has also briefed the president on the Iran blockade and ongoing war efforts, while tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz this week added fresh urgency.

Without a deal, U.S. and Israeli officials expect a week-long bombing campaign against Iran's leadership, energy facilities, nuclear sites and critical infrastructure, Axios reported. The next few days — spanning the U.S. midterms — may decide which track wins.

items.title: Binance hit by a $6.3 billion hack, the biggest theft in crypto history
items.summary:
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, says about $6.3 billion was taken in a security breach on Thursday — more than four times the $1.5 billion Bybit hack of 2025, the previous record. The exchange has suspended withdrawals while it rebuilds its withdrawal service, and says it will cover all losses from its SAFU insurance fund and company funds, insisting customer balances are safe.

Binance's initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave an attacker access to an internal service container used to submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions. The company says it found no evidence that wallet private keys leaked. Blockchain trackers estimate tens of thousands of coins moved across Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron networks, including about 204,500 ether from wallets used to back customer assets.

About $3 billion has been frozen on-chain so far with partners' help; Tether and Circle alone froze roughly $1.5 billion and $800 million. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs attributes the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, the North Korean state hacking unit the FBI blamed for the Bybit theft. Bitcoin fell about 5% in the early hours as the news spread, sliding from the $80,000 level toward $76,000 before steadying near $78,449.

Watch for Binance's promised technical post-mortem and whether withdrawals resume inside the 48-hour window co-founder Yi He suggested.

items.title: Alphabet shares plunge a record 12.6% as AI spending swallows its cash
items.summary:
Alphabet lost roughly half a trillion dollars of market value on Thursday after its third-quarter results missed expectations and showed the cost of its AI build-out accelerating. Shares fell 12.6% to $283.82 — a record one-day drop — as revenue of $127.58 billion came in just under the $127.96 billion forecast and earnings of $2.12 a share badly missed the $3.01 consensus.

The deeper worry is cash. Free cash flow swung to negative $9.07 billion, from a $24.46 billion inflow a year earlier, because capital spending hit $51.36 billion in a single quarter, mostly for AI infrastructure. Search revenue grew 12% to about $63 billion but missed estimates for a second straight quarter, fuelling the fear that AI chatbots and agents are starting to take the lucrative edge off Google Search — even as Google says search queries are growing at their fastest pace in five years. Cloud was the bright spot, roughly doubling to about $31 billion.

The selloff dragged the whole AI trade: the Nasdaq fell 1.4% on Thursday, communication services had their worst day since February 2022, and Asian tech markets followed lower on Friday, with Samsung and SK Hynix down around 5%.

Alphabet kept its full-year spending forecast at $195–205 billion and said it will rise significantly in 2027. The question hanging over the stock is when the spending starts paying for itself.

items.title: Microsoft's Azure cloud revenue jumps 48% to $33.2 billion
items.summary:
Microsoft gave investors a number they had asked about for a decade: Azure's actual dollar revenue. In the quarter ended September 30, Azure brought in $33.165 billion, up 48% from a year earlier — ahead of both analyst estimates and Microsoft's own guidance — under a new reporting structure that folds Azure together with its AI applications and agent platform.

The wider quarter was strong too. Total revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion, operating income rose 21% to $45.9 billion, and Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, up 30%. Capital spending was $45.2 billion, about three-quarters of it on short-lived gear such as CPUs and GPUs, yet the company still produced $18.6 billion of free cash flow. Management trimmed the calendar-year spending outlook to about $170 billion, citing delayed third-party capacity, and guided to Azure growth of 49–50% next quarter.

One concentration is worth watching: Microsoft booked $10 billion of revenue from its OpenAI arrangements in the quarter, about 11% of all revenue, and AI work now makes up roughly 30% of its $677 billion cloud backlog — a backlog whose growth is driven heavily by OpenAI, which signed a further $250 billion Azure commitment after the quarter closed.

In a week when Alphabet was punished for AI cash burn, Microsoft's mix — accelerating cloud revenue and positive cash flow — was the version of the AI story the market wanted to hear.

items.title: Amazon slips and Intel tumbles after earnings, despite strong cloud growth
items.summary:
Amazon's cloud unit had a strong quarter and its shares still fell. AWS sales grew 39.3% to $46 billion in the third quarter, accelerating from 37% growth the quarter before, but Amazon stock dropped about 7% in after-hours trading on Thursday as investors focused on how much cash the AI build-out is consuming and on a fourth-quarter sales forecast of $240–247 billion, straddling the $244.16 billion analysts expected.

Intel had the rougher night, falling about 18% in extended trading after a disappointing outlook. Together with Alphabet's record drop earlier in the day, the results hardened a pattern in this earnings season: revenue growth alone no longer protects a tech stock if the spending behind it outruns the cash coming in.

The contrast case sits across town. Microsoft stayed free-cash-flow positive while spending $45.2 billion on capital projects, and its shares rose about 5% after its report — evidence that the market is now grading each company's AI spending against the revenue already attached to it.

Friday's session will show whether the post-earnings slide spreads or stays confined to the names that missed.

items.title: U.S. economy grew 3.4% over the summer, but inflation is still running at 3.6%
items.summary:
The U.S. economy accelerated over the summer. Gross domestic product grew at a 3.4% annual rate from July through September, the Commerce Department reported Thursday, up from 2.2% in the spring and the strongest pace in a year. Consumer spending rose at a robust 3.8% clip for the second quarter running, business investment poured into AI data centres, and government spending rebounded.

The same morning brought the catch. Prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier — nearly double the Federal Reserve's 2% target — and the personal saving rate slipped to 3.8% from 4.1% in August. Adjusted for inflation, consumer spending was essentially flat in September, suggesting households are spending more largely because things cost more. The trade deficit was a major drag, shaving 3.3 percentage points off growth, and the federal deficit hit $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, about 6% of GDP.

Economists called it strong but fragile growth: powered by AI investment and wealthier households' spending, with hiring sluggish underneath. The report is the last major economic reading before Tuesday's midterms.

The Fed held rates steady at its October 27–28 meeting. With inflation sticky, analysts expect the strong headline number to buy the economy momentum into the fourth quarter, but not much room for the Fed to cut.

items.title: France's economy shrinks again as its debt worries deepen
items.summary:
France's economy contracted 0.1% in the third quarter, the national statistics agency Insee said Friday — its third straight quarter without growth, after stagnation in the spring and a 0.2% contraction at the start of the year. Economists had expected a small expansion. Household consumption rose 0.4%, but investment fell 0.6% and exports dropped 1.7%, dragging trade into negative territory.

The growth stall lands on top of a fiscal position that already worries markets. Public debt is close to 120% of GDP, the government expects a deficit of 5.4% of GDP in 2026 — far above the EU's 3% ceiling — and bond yields on French sovereign debt have climbed to multidecade highs amid deadlock in a fractured parliament. Inflation also accelerated, to 3.4% in October from 3.1% in September. The IMF this month cut its 2026 growth forecast for France to 0.4% and warned Paris to get its finances in order.

Finance Minister Roland Lescure warned that France is not in crisis but is "headed for a wall" if a deficit-reducing budget cannot be passed. Consumer confidence hit a 13-year low in October, and business surveys show the gloomiest outlook in six and a half years.

Europe's second-largest economy stalling matters beyond France: it limits how much support Paris can offer the wider eurozone, and it shapes the European Central Bank's room to move on rates.

items.title: Two helicopters collide in midair near an Oregon airport, killing all three aboard
items.summary:
Two helicopters collided in midair near McMinnville Municipal Airport, about 40 miles southwest of Portland, at about 2:15 p.m. on Thursday and crashed into a private farm field, killing all three people aboard. The aircraft were a 1995 Robinson R22 on a training flight and a 2018 Airbus AS350B3 on a maintenance flight.

Yamhill County Sheriff Sam Elliott identified the Robinson's occupants as Maddie Aasbo, a 22-year-old flight instructor from Texas, and a student pilot from the United Kingdom whose name is being withheld while family are notified through the consulate and the FBI. The Airbus's sole occupant was Tyler Sturdevant, 38, of nearby Newberg. Jerry Trimble Helicopters, the flight-training company whose aircraft was involved, said it is cooperating with investigators.

The crash closed Oregon Route 233 about a mile west of Dayton, and the sheriff's office asked residents to keep clear of the area. Witnesses described one helicopter crumpled in pieces and the other lying upside down in the field.

The National Transportation Safety Board will lead the investigation, with the FAA assisting. How two aircraft on routine daytime flights came to be in the same piece of sky — their paths, altitudes and communications — is not yet known, and a preliminary report typically takes weeks.

items.title: Record king tides flood streets from Southern California to South Florida
items.summary:
Exceptionally high king tides flooded coastal communities on both U.S. coasts this week, setting records between October 26 and 27. The full Hunter's Moon, near its closest point to Earth, lined up with record-warm ocean water and a strong El Niño to push tides 1.5 to 1.8 feet above predictions in Southern California.

Los Angeles Harbor's San Pedro gauge broke a record that had stood since 2005 — and dated back to 1923 — reaching about 8.18 feet on Tuesday. Newport Beach hit 8.4 feet and San Diego 8.14 feet, just over an inch short of its all-time mark. Flooding closed sections of Pacific Coast Highway and put streets and homes under water along the Los Angeles and Orange County coasts. In Florida, Miami's Virginia Key gauge recorded its highest non-hurricane water level ever, Port Canaveral set a non-tropical record, and Collins Avenue in Miami Beach, Las Olas Boulevard in Fort Lauderdale and Flagler Drive in West Palm Beach all flooded.

Coastal flood warnings stayed in effect through midweek from the Florida Keys to the Carolinas and down the California coast. Scientists describe the week as a preview: sunny-day flooding of this kind has become roughly twice as frequent over two decades as sea levels rise.

And this was not the seasonal peak. Higher astronomical king tides are expected around late November, again at Christmas, and again in mid-to-late January — with El Niño typically peaking over the winter.

items.title: Americans expect AI to grow the economy — just not their own job prospects
items.summary:
Americans think artificial intelligence will make the economy bigger. They are far less sure it will make room for them in it. That is the headline finding of the first Axios-CivicScience AI Sentiment Index, a new monthly tracker released Friday that scores public opinion across six measures, covering AI's effects on quality of life, society, jobs and growth, plus support for developing the technology and building data centres.

The anxiety is not evenly spread. In CivicScience's ongoing polling, 25% of employed adults say they are "very" concerned about how AI could affect their careers — and among people in technical roles, the group closest to the technology, the figure climbs to 40%. Separate polling this month also showed opinion of AI companies splitting along partisan lines.

The index arrives in the same week that AI spending dominated earnings season: Alphabet's record share plunge over cash burn, Microsoft's $677 billion cloud backlog, and a 3.4% GDP print powered in part by data-centre investment. The economy, in other words, is already running on AI money; the public's question is who the jobs go to.

Because the index is monthly, its value will build over time — the first edition sets the baseline for whether the "growth without jobs" feeling deepens or fades.

items.title: Top general puts it in writing: no plans for troops at polling places
items.summary:
The chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Gen. Dan Caine, has put in writing that the U.S. military has no plans to send federal troops or federalised National Guard to polling places in the midterms, and no plans to seize ballots, voting machines or other election materials. An assistant secretary echoed the position: election administration and security belong to state and local officials, not the armed forces.

The letters answer months of pressing by Senator Elissa Slotkin, who asked Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Caine for categorical written pledges after warning that a sudden federal role near Election Day could shake public trust. Hegseth, asked at an April hearing whether he would follow an order to seize ballots, called it a "gotcha hypothetical" and said he would not do anything illegal, but did not give the written promise Slotkin sought. The White House chief of staff has said the president would not use the military to suppress voting.

Separate reporting this week said National Guard units are being mobilised in all 50 states around the election — but with a mission focused on cybersecurity support for election infrastructure, alongside some observation roles that have drawn questions from senators.

The legal backdrop is the Posse Comitatus Act, which keeps the military out of civilian law enforcement unless Congress says otherwise. On the current record, there is no order or plan to put troops at the polls.

items.title: Only 28% of Americans see Pete Hegseth as a strong role model, poll finds
items.summary:
A new YouGov poll conducted for The Bulwark and the show Pablo Torre Finds Out asked Americans whether nine prominent men from politics, sports and entertainment count as strong role models for men. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth finished near the bottom: 28% said he is a strong role model, 39% said he is not — and among 18-to-29-year-olds, just 18% said yes against 34% no.

Hegseth was the second-lowest rated of the nine men, ahead of only President Trump, whom 55% said is not a strong role model against 37% who said he is. Former President Barack Obama topped the list, with 59% calling him a strong role model. The numbers land awkwardly for a Pentagon chief who has made masculine readiness a signature theme — directing fitness and grooming standards, and ordering annual testosterone-deficiency screening for male service members over 30.

Hegseth, an Army veteran of Iraq and Afghanistan and a former Fox News weekend host, has long drawn scrutiny over his stated views on women in combat roles, which he opposed in a 2024 podcast appearance.

Role-model polling is soft data, not a verdict on policy. But four days before a midterm election, it is another measure of how the administration's cultural pitch is landing with the young men both parties are courting.

items.title: Acton and Ramaswamy make their final pitch in a bruising Ohio governor's race
items.summary:
Ohio's governor's race — one of the nastiest in the country this year — is down to its final days. Democrat Amy Acton, who ran Ohio's health department under Governor Mike DeWine during the pandemic, is pitching a break from decades of Republican control: fully funded public schools and tax breaks for working Ohioans. Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, backed by President Trump, promises to eliminate the state income tax, roll back property taxes, scrutinise how Ohio runs its universities and end sanctuary cities.

The closing stretch has been dominated by a Ramaswamy ad that drew national attention and, by late October, was no longer running on Ohio airwaves; a Republican memo obtained by Axios said the ad was having a significant effect on the race, and a Suffolk University–USA Today poll found Ramaswamy's favourability down from the month before. Acton answered it from the stage of a Cleveland Public Auditorium rally headlined by former President Barack Obama — his first Ohio campaign stop in eight years — while Trump rallied for Ramaswamy in Chillicothe on October 28.

The affordability argument runs through both campaigns, down to the vehicles: Acton campaigns in a 2018 Jeep Cherokee, while finance reports show Ramaswamy has spent $41.3 million of his own money on the race, including more than $1 million on private jet travel.

Ohio picks its next governor on Tuesday, alongside a U.S. Senate race between Sherrod Brown and Jon Husted.

items.title: Early voting in Ohio tops 1.19 million, on pace to break the midterm record
items.summary:
Nearly 1.19 million Ohioans had already voted by Thursday, with days of early voting still to go, according to the Ohio Secretary of State's office. At the current pace, early turnout will pass the roughly 1.39 million early votes cast in the 2022 midterms — itself a record.

The partisan split in the early vote is striking. About 40% of Democratic-affiliated voters who requested ballots have cast them, compared with about 25% of Republican-affiliated voters: roughly 392,000 Democratic-affiliated ballots against 339,000 Republican-affiliated ones so far. The biggest group, though, is unaffiliated voters, who account for about 558,000 ballots — nearly double their number at this point in 2022. Election officials stress that early totals say who has voted, not how the races will finish, in a state that still leans Republican overall.

The practical rules matter this year: under a law signed last December, mail ballots must be received by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day, November 3 — there is no longer a grace period — and Secretary of State Frank LaRose has warned it is likely too late to mail one and have it arrive. Photo ID is required for in-person voting.

Early in-person voting runs today, 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., then Saturday 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and ends Sunday, November 1, from 1 to 5 p.m. There is no early voting on Monday.

items.title: Ohio voters will decide whether photo ID goes into the state constitution
items.summary:
The only statewide question on Ohio's ballot this year, Issue 3, asks voters to write the state's photo ID requirement for in-person voting into the Ohio Constitution. The rule already exists in state law, passed in 2022; the amendment would make it much harder for a future legislature or court to undo.

Also on Tuesday's ballot, two Ohio Supreme Court seats could leave the court entirely Republican, 7-0. Justice Jennifer Brunner, the court's lone Democrat, faces former Franklin County Judge Colleen O'Donnell, while Republican Justice Dan Hawkins faces Cincinnati appeals court Judge Marilyn Zayas. Republicans have won all six Supreme Court races since party labels were added to the ballot in 2022.

Statewide, Ohioans are also electing a governor, a U.S. senator, all 99 state House members, 17 state Senate seats and the other statewide executive offices — 139 races in all.

Polls are open Tuesday from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., and mail ballots must be in your county board of elections' hands by 7:30 p.m. that night to count.

items.title: Cleveland council refuses to repay the Browns $1.1 million for stadium repairs
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council voted 7-6 on Monday to reject reimbursing the Browns $1.1 million for emergency repairs to the city-owned lakefront stadium — money the city's lease obliges it to pay. Council members made little secret of the reason: frustration that the team is leaving downtown for a new domed stadium in Brook Park.

The work was not cosmetic. It covered a failed sanitary pump and sewer ejector pump, failed pipe insulation and an overhead door, among other fixes the Bibb administration said were needed to operate the stadium safely; officials warned that without them, pipes could freeze and sewage could back up this winter. The stadium, Huntington Bank Field, faces an estimated $117 million in potential repairs through 2034 and is expected to be demolished within five years of the team's departure, when the lease expires in 2028. The city still carries $18.6 million of stadium debt.

Council President Blaine Griffin, who voted to pay, has warned the team could sue the city over the lease. "We're being sold out," Council Member Michael Polensek told the administration, referring to the deal accepting $100 million from the Haslam Sports Group to drop lawsuits over the Brook Park move.

The Browns expect to be reimbursed eventually. Whether the standoff ends in a negotiated payment or in court, it is now part of the price of the move.

items.title: Browns get healthier for Sunday's first-place showdown in Pittsburgh
items.summary:
Thursday's injury report brought the Browns good news ahead of Sunday's trip to Pittsburgh, where the 5-2 Browns and 5-2 Steelers play for sole possession of first place in the AFC North. No new names were added to the report, and three key players were upgraded: centre Elgton Jenkins and edge rusher Jared Verse both returned to limited practice after sitting out Wednesday, and running back Dylan Sampson was a full participant, clearing concerns about his knee.

The one absence is starting right tackle Tytus Howard, still in concussion protocol. If he cannot clear it by Sunday, Dawand Jones is expected to start in his place. Friday's final report will set the official game statuses.

The week also brought a quieter storyline. Rookie receiver KC Concepcion — 30 catches for 315 yards through seven games — spoke Thursday about what it means that his media interviews, given while managing a speech impediment, have made him a role model for people facing their own obstacles. He told reporters he hopes speaking openly encourages others to push through theirs.

History is against Cleveland on Sunday: the Browns have won just three times in Pittsburgh since 1999 and have not won a regular-season game there in 23 years. Kickoff is 1 p.m. on CBS.

items.title: Kent State's president makes the case for Ohio's public universities
items.summary:
Kent State University President Todd Diacon is asking a question Ohio keeps circling: is college still worth it? His answer is yes — and he is making the case publicly for Ohio's public universities at a moment when their future is a live political fight in the governor's race.

In March, Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy cited declining enrolment among his reasons for proposing to consolidate some of the state's 14 public universities. That puts institutions like Kent State — and the smaller communities whose economies run through them — directly in the path of the election's outcome.

The argument for the defence looks at who actually gets to and through Ohio's colleges, and what supports or blocks them. Access and completion are not abstract policy for the families involved: they decide who gets to take the jobs Ohio says it wants to grow, and they shape the state's collective future.

Whoever wins on Tuesday inherits the question. Watch for whether consolidation talk becomes a concrete proposal in Columbus next year, and what it would mean for campuses across the region.

baby.tip: Dress-rehearse the hospital run: drive the route once together, note where to park and where to check in after hours, and keep the car topped up with fuel. With the car-seat base already installed, one calm practice trip now means the real one is just a drive, not a scramble.
baby.fact: A newborn's stomach is tiny at first — about the size of a cherry on day one and a walnut by day three — which is exactly why little-and-often feeds are the plan at the start. That small capacity grows fast over the first month.
